documents.title: NetFlow and Traffic Monitoring Standards
documents.body: Purpose How flow export is configured across the estate, and how the dashboard's traffic panel reads that data. What exports flow data Device class Protocol Export to Sampling Core routers IPFIX 10.20.5.11:2055 1:1 (unsampled) Distribution switches NetFlow v9 10.20.5.11:2055 1:1 Edge firewalls NetFlow v9 10.20.5.12:2055 1:1 Access switches none — — Access switches do not export flow. Their traffic is visible via SNMP interface counters, which is sufficient for capacity work and much cheaper. Keep flow unsampled on anything carrying WAN or internet traffic. Sampled flow is fine for volume trending but makes top-talker data misleading, which is exactly what you need it for during an incident. Active timeout matters Set the active flow timeout to 60 seconds. The default on most platforms is 30 minutes, which means a long-lived transfer is reported as one enormous flow when it finally ends, and your 5-minute graph shows a spike in the wrong interval. Cisco IOS-XE PRTG sensor configuration Add the flow sensor to the exporting device , not the collector. Match the sensor's port to the exporter's destination port (2055). Set Channel Selection to group by the traffic classes you actually report on. The dashboard plots one line per channel, so a sensor with 30 channels produces an unreadable chart. Enable at least one Toplist . Without it, the dashboard's Top Talkers panel has nothing to show — PRTG only retains top-talker data when a toplist is defined on the sensor. Recommended toplists Toplist Shows Use Top Talkers Busiest hosts "Who is saturating the link right now" Top Connections Busiest host pairs Finding a single runaway transfer Top Protocols Traffic by protocol Capacity planning and policy checks How the dashboard reads this The front page's Traffic by channel panel calls PRTG's historic-data API for the selected flow sensor and plots one line per channel. Two behaviours worth knowing: A channel named Total is dropped when per-channel data exists. Plotting a total alongside its own components double-counts the same traffic and flattens the components against the axis. Past eight channels, the remainder is summed into a single Other series. The categorical palette has eight slots, and cycling colours would make two different channels share one colour. Verification In PRTG the sensor should leave "No data" within two scan intervals of being created. If it stays empty, the export is not arriving — check that the exporter's source interface address is permitted by any ACL in the path, and that the probe's Windows Firewall allows inbound 2055/UDP. Related SNMP Configuration Baseline Triage a Down PRTG Sensor

documents.title: SNMP Configuration Baseline
documents.body: Purpose The SNMP settings every managed device must carry before it is added to PRTG. Standard Setting Value Version SNMPv3 (v2c only where v3 is unsupported) Auth protocol SHA-256 Privacy protocol AES-128 Username prtg-monitor Access Read-only, always Allowed source PRTG probe addresses only Port 161/UDP Location string <site>/<room>/<rack>/<RU> Read-write SNMP must not be enabled on any device. PRTG never needs it, and a read-write community is a device takeover waiting to happen. Why v3 v2c sends its community string in clear text, and that string is effectively a password for reading the whole device. Anyone on a span port, a mirrored uplink, or a compromised access switch can read it and then read your topology, interface names, ARP tables, and routing. Use v3 unless the device genuinely cannot do it. Where v2c is unavoidable: Use a community string unique to that device class, never public Restrict the source addresses to the probes in an ACL on the device Record the exception in the risk register with a replacement date Configuration Cisco IOS Windows Server SNMP on Windows is deprecated and v2c-only. Prefer WMI or a PRTG agent sensor for Windows hosts; use SNMP only where a third-party tool requires it. Linux (net-snmp) Verification From a PRTG probe server: Then in PRTG, run Recommended Sensors on the device and confirm it detects interfaces. If the walk works but PRTG times out, the probe is using different credentials than the ones you tested with — check the credential inheritance on the parent group. Related NetFlow and Traffic Monitoring Standards Triage a Down PRTG Sensor

documents.title: Password and Account Lockout Policy
headings: When a password must be reset immediately
documents.body: Scope All domain accounts, service accounts and local administrator accounts on company-managed systems. Requirements Setting Value Rationale Minimum length 14 characters Length beats composition rules Complexity requirement Disabled Encourages passphrases over P@ssw0rd1 Maximum age None for user accounts Forced rotation drives weaker choices Banned password list Enabled Blocks the leaked-password corpus MFA Required for all remote access Password alone is not sufficient Lockout threshold 10 attempts High enough to tolerate a stale credential Lockout window 15 minutes Lockout duration 15 minutes, auto-release Removes most unlock tickets Password reuse Last 24 blocked Expiry is deliberately disabled for user accounts. Mandatory rotation makes people pick predictable variants and write them down. Compromise response is a forced reset of the affected account, not a scheduled estate-wide one. Service accounts Use a Group Managed Service Account wherever the application supports it; the password is then managed by the domain and never known to anyone. Where a gMSA is not possible: 32 characters, random, stored in the password vault, rotated annually and on any team change. Service accounts must not be members of Domain Admins. Deny interactive sign-in for every service account. When a password must be reset immediately Any suspicion of compromise or phishing credential entry An account appearing in a breach notification Shared knowledge of the password, however it happened Staff departure where a shared credential existed Enforcement Settings are applied by the Default Domain Policy for the lockout values and by a Fine-Grained Password Policy for length and history. Service accounts sit in a separate FGPP with a longer minimum. Exceptions Exceptions require Information Security approval, a documented compensating control, and a review date no more than twelve months out. Record them in the risk register. Related Reset a Locked Active Directory Account Offboard a Departing Employee

documents.title: Server and Device Naming Convention
documents.body: Format NetBIOS still caps at 15 characters, so names stay short. Lowercase everywhere — DNS is case-insensitive, but mixed case in scripts and documentation is a steady source of mistakes. Server roles Prefix Role dc Domain controller fs File server sql SQL Server app Application server web Web server (IIS) prtg PRTG core or probe bkp Backup server hv Hyper-V host rds Remote Desktop host Network classes Prefix Class sw Switch rt Router fw Firewall ap Wireless access point ups UPS management card Site codes Code Site hq Head office br Branch (numbered per branch) dc Colocation wh Warehouse dc is both the domain-controller role prefix and the colocation site code. Role prefixes apply to servers and site codes to network and endpoint names, so the two never appear in the same position — but when scripting against names, match on the whole pattern, not a leading substring. Rules Never encode the operating system version or hardware model. Both change while the name stays, and a win2016 box running 2022 is worse than no information at all. Never reuse a retired name for twelve months. Stale DNS records, monitoring history and certificates all outlive the server. Numbers are zero-padded to two digits, so sorting works. The PRTG device name must match the DNS name exactly. The dashboard groups SNMP sensors by device name, and a mismatch splits one device into two. Verification Related Onboard a New Employee SNMP Configuration Baseline

documents.title: Role Access Templates
headings: Why not copy an existing user
documents.body: Purpose The group memberships each role gets at onboarding. Provision from this table, never by copying an existing user's account. Why not copy an existing user A copied account inherits every access grant the original picked up over years, including the ones granted for a project that ended. Those grants then propagate to the next copy. Within a few hires nobody can say why an account has the access it has, and access reviews become guesswork. Templates All staff Applied to every account regardless of role. Group Grants All-Staff Intranet, print queues, company shares VPN-Users Remote access, MFA enforced M365-E3 Licence assignment Finance Group Grants Finance-Staff Finance share, reporting portal ERP-Readers ERP read-only Printers-HQ-Floor2 Floor printers Finance approvers additionally need ERP-Approvers, which requires the finance director's written approval per person. Service Desk Group Grants Service-Desk-Operators Delegated AD unlock and password reset Helpdesk-Tools Remote assistance, asset register write PRTG-Read Monitoring read access Network Team Group Grants Network-Admins Switch and firewall management PRTG-Admins Monitoring configuration Change-Approvers Network change approval Network-Admins carries device configuration rights across the estate. Membership requires the network lead's approval and is reviewed quarterly. Review Every template group is reviewed quarterly by its owner. Memberships that cannot be justified against a current role are removed, not grandfathered. Related Onboard a New Employee Offboard a Departing Employee

documents.title: Triage a Down PRTG Sensor
headings: Decide what kind of failure it is
1. Is it only one sensor on the device?
2. Are all sensors on the device down?
3. Are all devices behind one probe down?
documents.body: Purpose Work out, quickly and in a fixed order, whether a red sensor on the dashboard means a real outage, a monitoring fault, or noise. Before you start Read access to PRTG The device's entry in the Server and Device Naming Convention so you know what it is before you touch it Decide what kind of failure it is Work top to bottom and stop at the first match. Is it only one sensor on the device? If every other sensor on the same device is green, the device is up and the problem is with that one check. Go to Sensor-level faults . Are all sensors on the device down? The device or the path to it is down. Go to Device-level faults . Are all devices behind one probe down? The probe service or its network path is the problem — not the devices. Check the PRTG probe service first; do not raise an incident per device. Sensor-level faults Message in PRTG Usual cause Action No such instance (SNMP error # 223) Interface index changed after a reboot or firmware update Re-scan the device and recreate the sensor SNMP timeout on one sensor only Device CPU saturated, or the OID is slow Raise the sensor's timeout and lower its scan rate Authentication failed SNMP community or v3 credentials changed Correct the credentials on the parent device Threshold exceeded Genuine condition Treat as a real alert Confirm the OID responds outside PRTG before changing anything: An interface index (ifIndex) is not stable across reboots on most switches. If traffic sensors break after every maintenance window, rebuild them against ifName or ifAlias instead of ifIndex. Device-level faults Check whether the device answers at all. If ICMP succeeds but SNMP fails, the agent is the problem, not the link: If ICMP fails, check the upstream device in PRTG's dependency tree before declaring the device down. A failed uplink shows as dozens of down devices. Confirm there is no change record covering the window before raising an incident. Escalation Condition Escalate to Core switch or router down Network Team lead, immediately Single access switch down Network Team, within the hour Monitoring fault only, service healthy Ticket, next business day Probe service down Monitoring owner, immediately Verification The sensor returns to green and stays green across at least three scan intervals. A sensor that flaps between up and down has not been fixed — treat flapping as still-open and look for duplex mismatch, a failing optic, or an undersized scan interval. Related NetFlow and Traffic Monitoring Standards SNMP Configuration Baseline

documents.title: Offboard a Departing Employee
headings: On the last working day, at the agreed time
documents.body: Purpose Revoke access, preserve data, and recover equipment when someone leaves, with a record that each step was completed. Before you start A Leaver Notification from HR with the last working day and time The manager's instruction on who inherits mailbox and file access Legal hold status for the account, if any Never delete a leaver's mailbox or home directory on the last day. Retention obligations usually require the data to survive the account. Disable first, delete only after the retention window. Procedure On the last working day, at the agreed time Disable the account and revoke active sessions. Revoke Microsoft 365 refresh tokens so existing sessions die immediately — disabling the account alone does not end a signed-in session. Move the account to the leavers OU so it drops out of the staff policies. Remove group memberships, keeping a record first. Convert the mailbox to shared and grant the nominated colleague access. Remove the licence only after the mailbox conversion has completed. Within five working days [ ] Recover laptop, phone, tokens, keys and access cards [ ] Wipe and re-image the device [ ] Transfer file ownership of personal drive contents to the manager [ ] Remove from on-call rotas, distribution lists and shared mailboxes [ ] Remove from third-party SaaS applications [ ] Close the asset register entries Verification Check Expected result Sign-in attempt Fails Get-ADUser jsmith -Properties Enabled, MemberOf Disabled, no groups VPN connection attempt Rejected Mail sent to the address Delivered to shared mailbox Asset register No open assignments Rollback If a departure is reversed within 30 days, re-enable the account, restore the group memberships from the saved list, and convert the mailbox back: Related Onboard a New Employee Password and Account Lockout Policy

documents.title: Onboard a New Employee
documents.body: Purpose Provision accounts, licences, hardware and access for a new starter, so they can work on day one. Before you start A completed New Starter Request from HR, including start date, job title, manager and cost centre The access template for the role (see Role Access Templates) An available Microsoft 365 licence Begin three business days before the start date. Hardware imaging and licence propagation are the two steps that most often run late. Procedure Create the directory account Add group memberships Use the role template rather than copying an existing user — copied accounts accumulate access that nobody can later justify. Assign licences and mailbox Wait for directory sync, or force it from the sync server: Assign the licence group in Microsoft 365 admin center. Confirm the mailbox exists before continuing — licence assignment is asynchronous and can take up to 30 minutes. Prepare hardware [ ] Image the device from the current Windows task sequence [ ] Join to the domain and confirm it lands in the right OU [ ] Enable BitLocker and verify the recovery key escrowed to AD [ ] Install the role software bundle [ ] Record the asset tag against the user in the asset register Hand over Provide the welcome sheet with the username, the first-sign-in steps, and the service desk contact details. Walk the user through MFA enrolment in person if they are on site. Verification Check Expected result Sign in to the new device Succeeds, prompts for password change Get-ADUser $sam -Properties MemberOf All template groups present Send and receive a test email Delivered both ways MFA enrolment Completed BitLocker recovery key in AD Present Rollback If a start date is cancelled, disable rather than delete the account for 30 days, then remove it: Related Offboard a Departing Employee Server and Device Naming Convention

documents.title: Reset a Locked Active Directory Account
documents.body: Purpose Unlock and, if required, reset the password for a domain account that has been locked out by the account lockout policy. Before you start Membership of Service Desk Operators (delegated unlock and reset rights) RSAT Active Directory tools, or a session on a domain controller An open ticket to record the action against Verify the caller's identity before unlocking any account. Use the callback number on record in the HR system — never a number supplied during the call. Procedure Confirm the lockout is real and find the source. Identify which domain controller recorded the lockout, so you know where to look for the source machine. Check event ID 4740 on that domain controller's Security log. The Caller Computer Name field names the device that triggered the lockout. Unlock the account. Only if the user cannot recall their password, force a reset: Tell the user which device caused the lockout. The usual culprits are a stale mapped drive, a phone with an old mail password, or a cached credential in Windows Credential Manager. Verification Check Expected result Get-ADUser jsmith -Properties LockedOut LockedOut : False User signs in on their own device Succeeds Repeat lockout within 15 minutes Does not occur If the account locks again immediately, the source device is still presenting the old password. Clear it before closing the ticket: Rollback Unlocking an account cannot be undone, and does not need to be. If a password was reset in error, the user sets a new one at next sign-in. Related Password and Account Lockout Policy Triage a Down PRTG Sensor
